**🔧 Bond tester update: smarter, more die-agnostic testing**

Sorry for the long post.

**TLDR**
- Neighbouring-bond short check removed
- New 10 µA and 1000 µA test currents for much clearer ESD diode detection
- Pseudo-Kelvin (3-wire) measurement: force and sense paths separated through the MUX
- Results simplified to OPEN / GOOD, the tester no longer judges shorts
- Power pads now tested via capacitor charging curve monitoring


**Design principle: the tester knows less* about die**

Two of these changes come from the same place. A generic tester shouldn't assume anything about the die under test:
- **Neighbour short check removed.** We previously used spare MUX channels to check neighbouring bonds. But we've already seen this backfire on a real die: one of the designs we tested has DVSS on adjacent pads, so a perfectly good die looks like it has a short. A generic tester can't distinguish "shorted by design" from "shorted by a bond defect," so the check is gone.
- **Results are now just OPEN or GOOD.** The tester confirms a bond exists by comparing the measurement against a wide acceptance threshold; it doesn't interpret the result in detail. For example, on analog designs an IO pad may be replaced with a power pad (e.g. GND) on an otherwise standard CoB board. Measuring that pad could look like a short to a supply rail, but it's by design, not a failure. So the tester now answers one question: is it an open, or not?

**Better ESD diode detection**
Added 10 uA and 1000 uA current sources alongside the existing one. Now have ~10uA, ~100uA, ~1000uA. They're simple resistor-based sources and not precision-calibrated, but that's fine for v1: this revision is a platform for us to learn on and improve our detection, and with the extra measurement points a diode is now much easier to detect.

**Pseudo-Kelvin measurement**
We had a free COM output on the MUX, so might as well put it to use: the force (current injection) and sense (ADC reading) paths are now separated through the MUX, instead of the ADC probing the current-source node directly. This removes the force-path MUX on-resistance from the measurement. It's not true 4-wire Kelvin, effectively 3wire: the return path is still shared through the MUX, so the return-leg R_on still contributes, as do the connector and its contact resistance. Fully removing those would need a separate sense contact per pad, and pogo pins would be a suitable way to achieve this 🤣. But let's try to leave that to next year. For our simple pass/fail testing, the current setup does the job.

**Power pads: capacitor charging curve**
Power pins used to cause trouble because of the decoupling capacitors on the PCB. Instead of fighting that, the tester now measures the charging curve itself: a good bond connects the pad to the die, whose ESD diode clamps the voltage before the capacitor charges fully. An open bond has no such clamp and lets it charge to full.


**What's next**
I expect there are still plenty of surprises waiting once we start bonding more CoBs. So far I've only managed to test a handful of different dies, and with new upcoming CoBs I expect the tool to fail in new ways, which is a good thing: every failure shows how to make the tester better and more universal.

Once the run 1 CoBs are done, we should be in a good position for an updated PCB design. Longer term, I'd like to keep improving the tester, with upgrading the current sources and the ADC at the top of the list.

If you have any questions or suggestions, please feel free to leave a reply  🙏

I'll see if I can find some COTS lasers that are more suited to fiber coupling than this <https://ams-osram.com/products/lasers/ir-lasers-vcsel/osram-bidos-e1005-l-plpvyl1-940a-e> (the cuboid is 500x500x1000 μm; the triangle of green circles are the three VCSEL diodes; this part is notable for being low cost and vaguely-decently couple-able into a cheap multimode fiber. "Should" just need a coupling lens on the end of the multimode fiber; it's `(1/e²)` beam divergence is given at 18° typ 25° max and reading the intensity plot in the datasheet the full width half maximum is about 8.5°), so I could try to approximately target having an on-die photodiode good for fiber data communications with a suitable low cost VCSEL diode transmitter. Notably vague ideas of brightness and less vague ideas of beam size and spectrum matter.

In case you weren't quite aware how photovoltaic mode works/acts: the PN diode when subjected to individual photons in it's absorption spectrum (AFAIK mostly this means "of energy exceeding the band gap but not far excessively so"; for silicon we're talking UV (A, probably B, maybe even C and somewhat exceeding that) to about 1000 nm. IIRC Nd:YAG's 1064nm is just a little too far.):
There is an inversion zone where charge carriers aren't nearly as free as in the notably doped p and n zones.
A photon hitting there knocks an electron out and spawns an electron/hole pair. Due to this very inversion zone those two charges drift off to the p and n zones, respectively. Electrons drift to the N side. 

This pair creation itself is essentially proportional to the incoming photons and mostly just cares about how likely it is for the photon to hit in this reception zone. One photon only creates one pair. 

If left open-circuit, these electrons on the N doped side accumulate until they discharge the very same way they would under regular forward bias conditions.
This is why solar cells have more output voltage in winter (diode forward voltage temp co) and why the external current at a fixed forward bias voltage drops when you apply more light: you're substituting the current with photocurrent.

If you want to see current go up as light goes bright, you'll have to reverse-bias the PN junction.
Note: the photocurrent from the light still flows the same direction through the "simplified small signal silicon PN diode model", but due to the forced inverted bias the bias current is now flipped in sign at the internal diode and thus the external view seems to be one of "current go up as light goes bright".
For response speed you btw. want to stay in reverse bias due to the inversion layer between the P and N widening and this reducing the capacitance (simple plate capacitor approximation).

Ideally you'd have been able to measure current flow proportional to brightness (as far as thermal conditions can be approximated as constant) _with the diode shorted into the current meter, i.e. 0V applied._

Could you just for clarity tell me what you meant exactly with the "measure with a multimeter at a fixed 1mA current"? Measure what? Current from where?

I do highly suggest to plan for getting e-test coverage for all reasonable layer configurations of photodiodes and photodiode-active structures (gate poly! thick oxide vs. thin oxide! threshold voltage options!) into Run3, though.
I can't do the muxed e-test alone, or if I could, I shouldn't.
If you mean what the foundry does -- then we don't control the e-test structures or data.
Aside from the optical access difficulties/specialties I'd see no reason it shouldn't be suitable for the task, though.
@namibj - If there is a choice, I would prefer you working on high speed SERDES and then packaging before random optical stuff 🙂

No, muxed E-test, a concept I hoped to get into delayed Run2; didn't manage; basically imagine roughly how the tiny tapeout analog tiles work.
Now re-size the cells to where the chip core area is 50% covered by VERY dense mux bus.
Two wires to each DUT via/"pin" to be able to use one as drive and the other as sense and also to further calibrate out variations in the mux itself.
Imagine just placing a lone SCL member there, except that it's flanked by fillcap's and then taps and then obligatory row end cells.
To be measured under DC/near-DC conditions and used with heavy spice modeling to find a statistical fit of things like extraction parameters and for SCL at least some fudge factors in how nearby structures interact, to represent how it all acts in practice.

Because they are way too high frequency for us to at all afford to do true dynamic tests of finer structures, so we might as well focus on doing good static/DC-op-point tests. Or at least static enough to see interesting behavior in something like a dynamic DFF.

Yeah; I've got the serdes 25G on SG13CMOS5L first and then in no implied order (I literally don't know ordering or amount of overlap) backport to gf180mcuD trying to get at least 10G out of that, and cross-port to sky130A trying to retain full 25G function even if it means fancier PCBs and a local retimer IC which is configured to mitigate limitations on the sky130A's analog high speed frontend performance.

Packaging is more limited by access and iteration count.

I'm not looking forward to doing optical stuffs for fun other than seeing towards appropriate test dies including something that vaguely looks suited to work for receiving a few hundred Mbit/s of data from a simple fiber directly into a gf180mcuD die.
You'll be my hero if you get anything which can do USB 5Gbit/s speed.
